content: An intrauterine device (IUD) is a contraceptive device placed inside the uterus. The term intrauterine refers to its location within the uterus. IUDs are among the most widely used reversible birth control methods globally, with approximately 160 million women using them. In China, IUDs are the most common form of contraception, surpassing sterilization. The device must be inserted and removed by a trained medical professional. Once in place, it remains effective for the duration of time pregnancy is not desired. Depending on the type, IUDs are approved for use for 5 to 10 years, with some, like the copper T380A, being effective for up to 12 years. Historically, early forms of IUDs were developed in the early 20th century. The first intrauterine device entirely contained within the uterus was described in 1909. In 1929, Dr. Ernst Gräfenberg introduced an IUD made of silk suture, reporting a 3% pregnancy rate among users. Later, in 1930, an improved version wrapped in silver wire was developed, though the wire was unknowingly contaminated with copper, which enhanced its contraceptive efficacy. Copper's role in improving IUD effectiveness was not recognized until decades later. In 1934, Japanese physician Tenrei Ota modified the Gräfenberg ring by adding a central supportive structure, reducing expulsion rates. However, high infection rates and political restrictions during World War II hindered further development. The first plastic IUD, the Margulies Coil, was introduced in 1958, but its large size caused discomfort for many users. In 1962, the smaller Lippes Loop gained popularity. In the 1970s, stainless steel single-ring IUDs were widely used in China due to their low manufacturing costs, but they were later banned due to high failure rates. In 1968, Dr. Howard Tatum in the USA designed the T-shaped plastic IUD, and shortly after, Dr. Jaime Zipper in Chile introduced the addition of copper to improve contraceptive effectiveness. Copper-containing IUDs could be made smaller, reducing side effects like pain and bleeding. T-shaped devices also had lower expulsion rates due to their similarity to the uterine shape. The poorly designed Dalkon Shield IUD, sold in the United States from 1971 to 1974, was associated with serious safety concerns, including septic spontaneous abortions and deaths, leading to its withdrawal from the market. Second-generation copper-T IUDs introduced in the 1970s had higher copper surface areas and achieved effectiveness rates exceeding 99%. Today, these are the most commonly available IUDs worldwide, except for newer frameless designs like the GyneFix. There are two main types of IUDs: copper-based (non-hormonal) and hormonal. In the United States, the copper ParaGard and the hormonal Mirena are available. In the UK, copper IUDs are referred to as IUDs, while hormonal devices are classified as intrauterine systems (IUS). Most non-hormonal IUDs have a T-shaped plastic frame wrapped with copper wire or collars. The GyneFix, a frameless IUD, is anchored to the uterine fundus with a suture. Copper-containing IUDs are named based on their copper surface area in square millimeters. Copper IUDs have failure rates of less than 1% per year, with cumulative 10-year failure rates of 2-6%. The presence of the device in the uterus triggers the release of leukocytes and prostaglandins, which are toxic to sperm and eggs. Copper enhances this spermicidal effect. However, IUDs do not protect against sexually transmitted infections (STIs) or pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). Copper IUDs are safe for use during breastfeeding. While the primary mechanism of action is spermicidal, some pro-life groups believe post-fertilization effects may contribute to their effectiveness, leading to debates about whether IUDs act as abortifacients. Contraindications for copper IUD insertion include pregnancy, postpartum sepsis, untreated cervical or endometrial cancer, unexplained vaginal bleeding, and current PID or purulent cervicitis. Women with metal sensitivities to copper or nickel may experience adverse reactions, though these are rare. Nulliparous women (those who have never given birth) may experience more side effects but can still use IUDs. Some providers prefer to insert IUDs during menstruation to confirm the absence of pregnancy, though insertion is safe at any time during the menstrual cycle if pregnancy is reasonably excluded. Side effects of IUD insertion include a transient increased risk of PID in the first 20 days, heavier and more painful menstrual periods, and rare complications like uterine perforation or expulsion. Expulsion is more common in younger women, nulliparous women, and those who have an IUD inserted immediately after childbirth or abortion. Women are advised to check the IUD strings monthly to ensure it remains in place. If pregnancy occurs with an IUD in place, there is an increased risk of miscarriage and preterm delivery, though these risks decrease if the IUD is removed after pregnancy is confirmed. Hormonal IUDs, such as the Mirena, reduce menstrual bleeding or prevent menstruation altogether and can treat heavy periods (menorrhagia). They release levonorgestrel, a progestogen, and are effective for up to five years. Hormonal IUDs may have some systemic side effects similar to other progestogen-only contraceptives, though at much lower levels. The frameless FibroPlant-LNG, still under development, is anchored to the uterine fundus like the GyneFix and has shown promising results in trials. The IUD is the most widely used reversible contraceptive method globally, with significant usage in countries like China, Russia, and Kazakhstan. In the United States, the ParaGard T380A was approved in 1984 and became available in 1988. Hormonal IUDs like the Mirena were first introduced in 1990 and remain a popular option for long-term contraception.
